content: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) is a condition affecting children under the age of one year. It can be treated surgically through either laparoscopic pyloromyotomy (LP) or open pyloromyotomy (OP). Since its introduction in 1990, LP has become increasingly common worldwide. This study aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of LP versus OP for the treatment of IHPS. A comprehensive literature search was conducted on February 4, 2021, to identify all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing LP and OP. The search included databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), as well as grey literature sources like Google and Google Scholar. Only RCTs and quasi-randomized trials were included in the analysis. Two independent reviewers screened the studies and extracted data. When data were missing, the authors of the original studies were contacted. A random-effects model was used to calculate risk ratios (RRs) for binary outcomes and mean differences (MDs) for continuous outcomes. The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The search identified 434 records, of which 410 unique publications were screened after removing duplicates. Seven RCTs, reported in eight publications, were included in the final analysis. These studies involved a total of 720 participants, with 357 undergoing OP and 363 undergoing LP. The studies were conducted in various countries, including the USA, France, Japan, Bangladesh, and a multi-country trial. The evidence suggests that LP may lead to a slight increase in the risk of mucosal perforation compared to OP. The risk ratio for mucosal perforation was 1.60 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.49 to 5.26), based on data from seven studies with 720 participants. This corresponds to an estimated increase of up to five additional cases of mucosal perforation per 1,000 participants, although the confidence interval ranges from four fewer to 44 more cases per 1,000 participants. The certainty of this evidence was rated as low. Four RCTs involving 502 participants reported on the risk of incomplete pyloromyotomy. The data suggest that LP may increase the risk of incomplete pyloromyotomy compared to OP, but the confidence interval includes the possibility of no difference (RR 7.37, 95% CI 0.92 to 59.11). In the LP group, six cases of incomplete pyloromyotomy were reported among 247 participants, while no cases were reported in the OP group (255 participants). The certainty of this evidence was also low. All seven studies (720 participants) reported on postoperative wound infections or abscess formation. The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effect of LP on these outcomes compared to OP (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.24 to 1.45). Similarly, the evidence is very uncertain about the effect of LP on the risk of postoperative incisional hernia (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.11 to 9.53; 4 studies, 382 participants). Five RCTs, including 562 participants, assessed the length of hospital stay. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of LP compared to OP on this outcome (MD −3.01 hours, 95% CI −8.39 to 2.37 hours). Six studies, involving 622 participants, evaluated the time to full feeds. Again, the evidence is very uncertain about the effect of LP compared to OP (MD −5.86 hours, 95% CI −15.95 to 4.24 hours). The operating time was also assessed in six studies with 622 participants, and the evidence remains very uncertain (MD 0.53 minutes, 95% CI −3.53 to 4.59 minutes). In conclusion, LP may result in a small increase in the risk of mucosal perforation compared to OP for the treatment of IHPS. There may also be an increased risk of incomplete pyloromyotomy with LP, but the evidence is imprecise and includes the possibility of no difference. The effects of LP compared to OP on other outcomes, such as the need for re-operation, postoperative wound infections, abscess formation, hematoma or seroma formation, incisional hernia, length of hospital stay, time to full feeds, and operating time, remain uncertain due to the very low certainty of the evidence. The certainty of the evidence was downgraded for most outcomes due to study design limitations and imprecision. Overall, there is limited evidence comparing LP and OP for IHPS, and the studies did not provide sufficient information to assess the impact of surgeon training, experience, or preferences on the outcomes.
